title: Traffic-related air pollution and respiratory symptoms among asthmatic children, resident in Mexico City: the EVA cohort study.
ehr_evidence: The study relied on daily symptom diaries filled out by mothers, environmental monitoring from the Mexico City government fixed-site stations (RAMA) and school-based Mini-Vol and Ogawa passive samplers, and traffic counts; medical records were consulted only for allergy test results, medication, and medical visits during the 2 preceding years.
summary: A prospective panel study of 147 asthmatic and 50 healthy children aged 6-14 years in Mexico City followed for an average of 22 weeks, associating traffic-related air pollution exposure (PM2.5, NO2, O3, vehicle counts) with daily respiratory symptoms and bronchodilator use.
key_findings: An increase of 17.4 μg/m3 (IQR) of PM2.5 (24-h average) was associated with an 8.8% increase in wheezing (95% CI: 2.4% to 15.5%).
An increase of 34 ppb (IQR) of NO2 (1-h maximum) was associated with a 9.1% increase in wheezing (95% CI: 2.3% to 16.4%).
An increase of 48 ppb (IQR) of O3 (1-hr maximum) was associated with a 10% increase in wheezing (95% CI: 3.2% to 17.3%).

Diesel-fueled motor vehicles were significantly associated with wheezing (IRR = 1.29; 95% CI: 1.03 to 1.62) and bronchodilator use (IRR = 1.32; 95% CI: 0.99 to 1.77) for an increase of 130 vehicles hourly.
The incidence of coughing was 3 times greater among asthmatic than healthy children (IRR = 3.1; 95% CI: 2.8 to 3.4) and wheezing 8 times greater (IRR = 8.5; 95% CI: 6.4 to 11.4).
Among healthy children, a significant association was observed between NO2 and coughing (OR = 1.22; 95% CI: 1.03 to 1.45) but no significant association between PM2.5 or O3 and respiratory symptoms.
Traffic density was significantly related to respiratory symptoms in asthmatic children (IRR = 1.88; 95% CI: 1.14 to 3.09 for an IQR of 499 vehicles of SBPT).
The risk of wheezing decreased significantly with greater distance from the main road (IRR = 0.69; 95% CI: 0.49 to 0.98 for an increase of 212 m).
PM2.5 absorbance was positively but not significantly associated with coughing (OR = 1.55; 95% CI: 0.89 to 2.69) and wheezing (OR = 1.50; 95% CI: 0.83 to 2.72).
captured_features: Daily symptom records (coughing, wheezing, breathing difficulty)
Traffic density and vehicle counts by fuel type
Distance from main road to residence
Environmental tobacco smoke, pets, carpet at home
population: 147 asthmatic and 50 healthy children aged 6-14 years resident in Mexico City
exposure_domain: Traffic-related air pollution (PM2.5, NO2, O3, diesel exhaust, vehicle traffic)
limitations: Environmental exposure was evaluated using RAMA central monitoring locations, potentially causing misclassification.
Participants were selected on a voluntary basis and were not representative of the asthmatic and healthy population of Mexican children.
Small sample size for the PM2.5 absorbance subanalysis.
High correlation between traffic classes (coefficient of correlation 0.5 to 0.7) complicating separation of vehicle-type effects.
